title: NPS explained: tiers, tax benefits and what you get at 60
seoTitle: NPS Tax Benefit 2026: Old vs New Regime, 80% Rule
h1: NPS explained: tiers, tax benefits and what you get at 60
metaDescription: NPS tax benefit for 2026: the ₹50,000 deduction (old regime only), employer NPS in the new regime, the December 2025 exit rules and the 80% lump-sum tax catch.
excerpt: The extra ₹50,000 works only in the old regime; in the new one, employer NPS is the lever. What you get at 60 under PFRDA's December 2025 rules, and why only 60% of the corpus is still tax-free.
targetAudience: Indian salaried employees considering NPS for tax and retirement
sourceVideoTitle: All NPS Changes Explained in 8 Minutes (2026 Rules)

author: Muthu

faq.question: Can I claim the extra ₹50,000 NPS deduction in the new tax regime?
faq.answer: No. The extra ₹50,000 for your own NPS contribution is available only under the old regime. In the new regime, the only NPS deduction is for your employer's contribution, up to 14% of your basic salary plus DA. If you've moved to the new regime, ask whether your employer offers corporate NPS.

faq.question: Is the NPS lump sum at 60 tax-free?
faq.answer: Only 60% of the corpus is tax-free. The December 2025 rules let non-government subscribers withdraw up to 80% as a lump sum, but the tax exemption wasn't extended; the extra 20% is taxed at your slab rate, and the annuity's pension is taxed as income when you receive it.

faq.question: How much of my NPS must go into an annuity now?
faq.answer: For non-government subscribers with more than ₹12 lakh at exit, at least 20%. With ₹8–12 lakh, you can take up to ₹6 lakh as a lump sum and spread the rest over at least six years or buy an annuity. With ₹8 lakh or less, you can withdraw everything. Government employees still annuitise at least 40%.

faq.question: What's the difference between NPS Tier I and Tier II?
faq.answer: Tier I is the locked pension account that carries the tax benefits. Tier II is an optional, flexible account you can withdraw from any time, but it generally has no tax benefit, except a Tier II "Tax Saver" variant with a three-year lock-in. You need a Tier I account to open Tier II.

faq.question: Can I withdraw from NPS before 60?
faq.answer: Partly. You can withdraw up to 25% of your own contributions for specified purposes, up to four times before 60 with four-year gaps, and you can now take a loan against NPS. Accounts opened by individuals can also exit normally after 15 years. Leaving earlier than that means a much larger share goes into an annuity.
